source_text: Unum uerum deum omnipotentem, ex quo omnia, per quem omnia. in quo omnia, et rogaui et rogo, ut in refellenda et reuincenda haeresi uestra, Manichaei. cui et uos fortasse inprudentius quam malitiosius adhaesistis, det mihi mentem pacatam atque tranquillam et magis de uestra correctione quam de subuersione cogitantem. quamquam enim dominus per suos seruos regna subuertat erroris, ipsos tamen homines, in quantum homines sunt, emendandos esse potius quam perdendos iubet. et quicquid diuinitus ante illud ultimum iudicium uindicatur, siue per inprobos siue per iustos siue per nescientes siue per scientes siue occulte siue palam: non ad interitum hominum, sed ad medicinam ualere credendum est; quam qui respuerint, extremo subplicio praeparantur. quapropter cum in hac uniuersitate rerum alia sint, quae ualent ad corporalem uindictam, sicut ignis et uenenum et morbus et cetera huiusmodi, alia, quibus apud se ipsum non molestiis corporis sui, sed cupiditatum suarum laqueisan imus puniatur, sicut est damnum, exilium, orbitas, contumelia et his similia; quaedam uero non sint cruciamenta, sed quasi fomenta et lenimenta languentium, ut sunt consolationes, cohortationes, disputationes et quaecumque sunt alia: horum omnium quaedam etiam per malos nescientes operatur summa dei iustitia, quaedam autem per scientes bonos. nostrum igitur fuit eligere et optare meliora, ut ad uestram correctionem aditum haberemus, non in contentione et aemulatione et persecutionibus, sed mansuete consolando, beniuole cohortando, leniter disputando. sicut scriptum est: seruum autem domini non oportet litigare, sed mitem esse ad omnes, docibilem, patientem, in modestia corripientem diuersa sentientes. nostrum ergo fuit uelle has partes expetere; dei est uolentibus et petentibus donare, quod bonum est.
thought_title: Prayer for a peaceful mind in refuting Manichaean heresy
orientation: Augustine opens the treatise by praying to the one true God and explaining that he seeks the correction, not the destruction, of the Manichaeans.
pass_a_gloss: The one true almighty God, from whom are all things, through whom are all things, in whom are all things, I have both asked and I ask, that in refuting and disproving your heresy, Mani, to which you too have perhaps adhered more imprudently than maliciously, he may give me a mind made peaceful and tranquil and thinking more about your correction than about your overthrow. For although the Lord through his servants overthrows the kingdoms of error, yet he commands that the men themselves, insofar as they are men, are to be amended rather than destroyed. And whatever is divinely avenged before that final judgment, whether through wicked men or through just men, whether through those who do not know or through those who know, whether secretly or openly, it is to be believed that it avails not for the destruction of men but for their medicine; those who have rejected this are being prepared for the final punishment. Wherefore since in this whole universe of things some things are such as avail for bodily punishment, like fire and poison and disease and other things of this kind, other things by which the mind is punished within itself not by troubles of its body but by snares of its own desires, such as is loss, exile, bereavement, insult, and things similar to these; and some things are not torments but as it were fomentations and soothing remedies for the sick, such as are consolations, exhortations, disputations, and whatever other things there are: of all these things, some the highest justice of God works even through evil men who do not know, but some through good men who know. Therefore it was ours to choose and to desire the better things, so that we might have an approach to your correction, not in contention and rivalry and persecutions, but by consoling gently, by exhorting kindly, by disputing softly. As it is written: but the servant of the Lord must not quarrel, but be gentle toward all, teachable, patient, correcting in modesty those who think differently. Therefore it was ours to wish to seek these parts; it is God's to give what is good to those who will and ask.

choices.term: ex quo omnia, per quem omnia, in quo omnia
choices.english: from whom are all things, through whom are all things, in whom are all things
choices.why: Preserves the threefold prepositional structure and the theological formula exactly, with the relative pronouns referring to God.
rejected: from whom all things, through whom all things, in whom all things

choices.term: in refellenda et reuincenda haeresi uestra
choices.english: in refuting and disproving your heresy
choices.why: The gerundives express purpose and ongoing action; 'disproving' captures reuincenda as a stronger, conclusive refutation.
rejected: in refuting and convicting your heresy
in the refutation and disproof of your heresy

choices.english: a mind made peaceful and tranquil
choices.why: The perfect passive participles describe the state Augustine asks God to produce in his mind; 'made peaceful' preserves the passive force.

choices.english: are to be amended rather than destroyed
choices.why: The gerundives express obligation; 'amended' keeps the moral correction sense of emendare, and 'destroyed' the strong sense of perdere.
rejected: are to be corrected rather than ruined
should be improved rather than lost

choices.why: Medicina is a key metaphor for Augustine's view of divine punishment as healing; 'medicine' preserves the image.

choices.english: fomentations and soothing remedies for the sick
choices.why: Fomenta and lenimenta are medical terms for warm applications and soothing agents; the literal rendering keeps the therapeutic imagery.
rejected: comforts and reliefs for the weak
poultices and balms for the ailing

bible_refs.note: seruum autem domini non oportet litigare, sed mitem esse ad omnes, docibilem, patientem, in modestia corripientem diuersa sentientes

pass_b_english: I have prayed, and I still pray, to the one true almighty God, from whom are all things, through whom are all things, in whom are all things, that in refuting and disproving your heresy, Mani—to which you have perhaps attached yourselves more imprudently than maliciously—he would give me a mind made peaceful and tranquil, one that thinks more about your correction than about your overthrow. For although the Lord overthrows the kingdoms of error through his servants, he commands that the people themselves, insofar as they are people, are to be amended rather than destroyed. And whatever is divinely avenged before that final judgment—whether through the wicked or the righteous, whether through the ignorant or the knowing, whether secretly or openly—we must believe that it avails not for the destruction of human beings but for their medicine. Those who reject that medicine are being prepared for the final punishment.

Therefore, since in this whole universe of things some things have power for bodily punishment, such as fire, poison, disease, and others of this kind, and other things by which the soul is punished within itself not by troubles of its body but by the snares of its own desires, such as loss, exile, bereavement, insult, and things like these, while still other things are not torments but rather fomentations and soothing remedies for the sick, such as consolations, exhortations, disputations, and whatever else there may be—of all these, the highest justice of God works some even through the wicked who do not know what they do, and others through the good who do know. It was ours, then, to choose and desire the better things, so that we might have access to your correction, not in contention and rivalry and persecutions, but by consoling gently, exhorting kindly, disputing mildly. As it is written: "The Lord's servant must not quarrel, but be gentle to everyone, teachable, patient, correcting opponents with gentleness" (2 Timothy 2:24–25). It was ours, then, to want to seek this part; it is God's to grant what is good to those who will and ask.

problems.source_quote: seruum autem domini non oportet litigare, sed mitem esse ad omnes, docibilem, patientem, in modestia corripientem diuersa sentientes
problems.why: The Latin quoted matches 2 Timothy 2:24-25, but the English citation says only 2:24 while quoting text from both verses.
problems.ruling: Latin includes 'in modestia corripientem diuersa sentientes' from 2 Tim 2:25; citing only 2:24 misleads readers about the scriptural reference.

fixed: The citation should cover both verses quoted: the Latin matches 2 Timothy 2:24-25, so the citation is updated to 2 Timothy 2:24–25.

last_rejected.quote: the soul is punished within itself not by troubles of its body but by the snares of its own desires
last_rejected.source_quote: quibus apud se ipsum non molestiis corporis sui, sed cupiditatum suarum laqueis animus puniatur
last_rejected.why: Source has 'animus' (mind/soul) as subject; English inserts 'the soul' and drops 'animus' as the one punished.
last_rejected.fix: by which the mind is punished within itself not by troubles of its body but by the snares of its own desires
last_rejected.ruling: English 'the soul is punished' captures 'animus puniatur' accurately; 'animus' is subject in both, just rendered as 'soul' rather than 'mind'.

last_rejected.why: In this Old Latin form of 2 Timothy 2:24, docibilem means able to teach, not teachable.
last_rejected.fix: but be gentle to everyone, able to teach, patient, correcting with gentleness those who think differently
last_rejected.ruling: In 2 Tim 2:24 Vulgate/Old Latin 'docibilem' renders Greek didaktikon ('apt to teach'); 'teachable' is a possible but wrong-leaning sense, yet within range of the Latin and not meaning-changing in context.
